source_text:
οὗτος παράδεισος ἀληθῶς τρυφῆς, αὕτη ἀληθὴς εὐφροσύνη καὶ τρυφή, ἣν ἐτρυφήσαμεν ἐν τῷ διηνυσμένῳ τῷδε χρόνῳ, καὶ οὐκ ὀλίγῳ ἤδη, καὶ ὀλίγῳ πάντη, εἰ μέχρι τούτου στήσεται, ἀπελθοῦσιν ἤδη καὶ ἀναχωρήσασιν ἐντεῦθεν. οὐκ οἶδα γὰρ τί παθών, ἢ πάλιν ἁμαρτών, ἐκπορεύομαι, ἐξελαύνομαι. τί χρὴ λέγειν, ἀγνοῶ, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι δεύτερος ἐκ παραδείσου Ἀδὰμ ἐγώ, καὶ λαλεῖν ἠρξάμην. ὡς καλῶς εἶχον ἀκούων λέγοντος διδασκάλου, καὶ σιωπῶν. ὡς ὄφελον καὶ νῦν ἡσυχίαν ἄγειν. ἐμάνθανον σιωπῶν, ἀλλὰ μὴ τὸ καινὸν τοῦτο θέαμα ἀκροατὴν τὸν διδάσκαλον ποιήσασθαι. τί γάρ μοι ἔδει τῶν λόγων τούτων; τί δὲ καὶ προσφθέγγεσθαι τοιαῦτα; μὴ ἀπιέναι, προσκαρτερεῖν δέ, δέον. ἀλλὰ τῆς παλαιᾶς ἀπάτης ἔοικεν εἶναι ταῦτα πλημμελήματα, τῶν τε ἀρχαίων δίκαι αἵδε με μένουσιν ἔτι. ἢ καὶ αὖθις ἀπειθεῖν μοι δοκῶ, ὑπερβαίνειν τολμῶν τοὺς λόγους τοῦ Θεοῦ, μένειν δέον ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ πρὸς αὐτοῖς. ὃ δὲ ἄπειμι, φεύγων μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς μακαρίας ταύτης ζωῆς, οὐχ ἧττον, ἢ ἀπὸ προσώπου Θεοῦ ὁ παλαιὸς ἐκεῖνος ἄνθρωπος, εἰς δὲ τὴν γῆν ἐπιστρέφων ἐξ ἧς ἐλήφθην. γῆν τοιγαροῦν ἔδομαι, πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς μου, καὶ γῆν ἐργάζομαι, καὶ ταύτην ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους ἀνατέλλουσάν μοι, τὰς ἐμὰς λύπας καὶ φροντίδας τὰς ἐπονειδίστους, ἀφέμενος τῶν καλῶν καὶ ἀγαθῶν φροντίδων. καὶ ἃ καταλέλοιπα πρὸς ταῦτα πάλιν ἐπιστρέφων τὴν γῆν ὅθεν ἐξῆλθον, καὶ τὴν συγγένειαν τὴν ἐμὴν κάτω, καὶ εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου. ἀπολιπὼν γῆν τὴν ἀγαθήν, ἔνθα μοι οὖσα ἡ ἀγαθὴ πατρὶς ἠγνοεῖτο πάλαι· καὶ συγγενεῖς οὓς ἔχων ψυχῆς ἐμῆς οἰκείους, ὕστερον γινώσκειν ἠρξάμην· καὶ τὸν οἶκον τοῦ ἀληθῶς πατρὸς ἡμῶν, ἐν ᾧ μένων, ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ μένειν θελόντων υἱῶν τῶν ἀληθῶν, σεμνῶς τιμᾶται καὶ γεραίρεται ὁ πατήρ. ἐγὼ δὲ ἄσεμνος καὶ ἀνάξιος ἐξέρχομαι τῶν δὴ στραφεὶς εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, καὶ παλινδρομῶν. λέγεταί τις υἱὸς παρὰ πατρὸς ἀπολαβὼν τὸ ἐπιβάλλον αὐτῷ πρὸς ἕτερον αὐτοῦ ἀδελφὸν κλῆρον, ἀποδημῆσαι τοῦ πατρὸς εἰς χώραν μακρὰν θελήσας τοῦτο. ζῶν δὲ ἀσώτως, διασκορπίσαι τὴν πατρῴαν οὐσίαν καὶ καταναλῶσαι. τέλος δὲ κατ᾽ ἀπορίαν, ἑαυτὸν μισθώσας συφορβεῖν. ὑπὸ λιμοῦ δὲ ἀναγκαζόμενος καὶ κοινωνεῖν τῶν τροφῶν τοῖς χοίροις ἐπιθυμεῖν μέν, μὴ τυγχάνειν δὲ μηδὲ τούτου. δίκην οὖν ἐκτίσαι τῆς ἀσώτου αὐτῷ τραπέζης, τῆς πατρικῆς οὔσης βασιλικῆς ἀμειψάμενος, ἃς οὐ προεῖδε, τὰς χοιρείους καὶ τὰς ἐν θητείᾳ τροφάς. τοιοῦτόν τι πείσεσθαι ἐοίκαμεν ἀπελθόντες, καὶ οὐδὲ σὺν παντὶ τῷ ἐπιβάλλοντι κλήρῳ. οὐδὲ γὰρ λαβόντες ἃ ἐχρῆν· ἄπιμεν δὲ ὅμως. τὰ μὲν καλὰ καὶ φίλα καταλιπόντες μετὰ σοῦ καὶ παρὰ σοί, ἀμειψάμενοι δὲ τὰ χείρω. διαδέξεται γὰρ ἡμᾶς σκυθρωπὰ πάντα, θόρυβος καὶ ταραχὴ ἐξ εἰρήνης, καὶ ἐξ ἡσύχου καὶ εὐτάκτου, βίος ἄτακτος. ἐκ δὲ ἐλευθερίας ταύτης, δουλεία χαλεπή, ἀγοραὶ καὶ δίκαι, καὶ ὄχλοι καὶ χλιδή, καὶ σχολὴ μὲν ἡμῖν οὐκέτι πρὸς τὰ κρείττω οὐδ᾽ ἡτισοῦν. οὐδὲ λόγια τὰ θεῖα λαλήσομεν· λαλήσομεν δὲ τὰ ἔργα τῶν ἀνθρώπων. (τοῦτο δὴ καὶ ἁπλῶς ἀρά τις εἶναι νενόμισται ἀνδρὶ προφήτῃ.) ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ πονηρῶν ἀνθρώπων. νὺξ ὄντως ἐξ ἡμέρας, ἐκ δὲ λαμπροῦ φωτὸς σκότος, καὶ ἐκ πανηγύρεως πένθος, καὶ ἐκ πατρίδος πολεμία χώρα διαδέξεται ἡμᾶς, ἐν ᾗ ᾠδὴν μὲν ἱερὰν οὐκ ἔξεστί μοι ᾄδειν. πῶς γὰρ ἐν γῇ ἀλλοτρίᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς μου; ἔνθα μένοντας οὐκ ἔστι προσᾶσαι Θεῷ. κλαίειν δὲ μόνον καὶ στένειν ὑπομιμνησκόμενοι τῶν ἐνθάδε, εἰ καὶ τοῦτό μοί τις συγχωρήσεται. πολέμιοί ποτε λέγονται ἐπελθόντες πόλει μεγάλῃ καὶ ἱερᾷ, ἐν ᾗ τὸ θεῖον ἐθεραπεύετο, αἰχμαλώτους κατασῦραι τοὺς ἐνοικοῦντας καὶ ὑμνῳδοὺς καὶ θεολόγους εἰς τὴν αὐτῶν χώραν, Βαβυλωνία δὲ ἦν, τοὺς δὴ ἐνεχθέντας εἰς αὐτήν, μηδ᾽ ἀξιουμένους ὑπὸ τῶν κρατούντων, ὑμνεῖν ἐθέλειν τὸ θεῖον, μηδὲ ψάλλειν ἐν τῇ βεβήλῳ. ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ὄργανα τὰ μουσικά, κρεμάσαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἰτεῶν ἀργήσαντας, αὐτοὺς δὲ κλαίειν ἐπὶ τῶν ποταμῶν Βαβυλῶνος. ἐκείνων τις εἶναι δοκῶ ἐξελαυνόμενος ἀπὸ πόλεως, καὶ πατρίδος ἐμῆς ταύτης καὶ ἱερᾶς, ἔνθα μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν τε καὶ νύκτα, οἱ ἱεροὶ ἀπαγγέλλονται νόμοι, ὕμνοι τε καὶ ᾠδαί, καὶ λόγοι μυστικοί. καὶ φῶς τὸ ἡλιακὸν καὶ τὸ διηνεκὲς ἡμέρας ὕπαρ, ἡμῶν προσομιλούντων τοῖς θείοις μυστηρίοις, καὶ νυκτὸς ὧν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εἶδέ τε καὶ ἔπραξεν ἡ ψυχή, ταῖς φαντασίαις κατεχομένων. καὶ ὅλως συνελόντα εἰπεῖν, ἔνθα ἡ ἔνθεος διὰ παντὸς κατακωχή, ταύτης ἐξελαύνομαι, αἰχμάλωτος φερόμενος εἰς τὴν ἀλλοτρίαν γῆν. ἔνθα μοι οὔτε αὐλεῖν ἐξέσται, κρεμασαμένῳ τὸ ὄργανόν μου ὥσπερ κἀκείνοις ἀπὸ τῶν ἰτεῶν. ἀλλ᾽ ἐν μὲν τοῖς ποταμοῖς ἔσομαι, πηλὸν δὲ ἐργάσομαι, καὶ ὕμνους λέγειν οὐκ ἐθελήσω, μεμνημένος· ἀλλ᾽ ἴσως ὑπὸ μακροεργίας τῆς ἄλλης, καὶ ἐπιλήσομαι, συληθεὶς κατὰ τὰς μνήμας.

Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀπιών, ἄκων μόνον ὥσπερ αἰχμάλωτος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑκὼν ἄπειμι, οὐχ ὑπ᾽ ἄλλου του, ὑπ᾽ ἐμαυτοῦ δὲ ἐκπεπολεμημένος, ἐξὸν μένειν τάχα. καὶ ἀπιὼν ἐντεῦθεν, οὐκ ἀσφαλῶς πορεύσομαι, ὡς ἀπὸ ἀσφαλοῦς καὶ εἰρηνευομένης τινὸς πόλεως ἐξελθών. εἰκὸς δὲ ὡς ἄρα ὁδοιπορῶν, καὶ λῃσταῖς συντεύξομαι καὶ συλληφθήσομαι, καὶ γυμνωθεὶς τρωθήσομαι τραύμασι πολλοῖς, καὶ κείσομαί που ἡμιθνὴς ἐρριμμένος.
thought_title: Driven from paradise: Adam, the prodigal, and Babylon
orientation: Leaving Origen's school, Gregory compares himself to Adam driven from paradise, to the prodigal son and to the exiles in Babylon.
pass_a_gloss: This truly a παράδεισος of τρυφή (paradise of delight); this true εὐφροσύνη (gladness) and τρυφή, which we enjoyed in this completed time, not short already, and short altogether, if it will stop here, for us now departing and withdrawing from here. For I do not know what having suffered, or again having sinned, I go out, I am driven out. What I must say I do not know, except that a second Adam out of paradise am I, and I began to talk. How well I was, hearing a teacher speaking, and being silent. Would that even now to keep quiet. I was learning being silent, but not to have made this new spectacle: the teacher a hearer. For what need of these words? What also to address such things? Not to depart, but to persevere, being needed. But these offenses seem to be of the old deception, and these penalties of the ancient [things/ones] still await me. Or again I seem to disobey, daring to overstep the words of God, needing to remain in them and by them. Wherefore I depart, fleeing from this blessed life, not less than from the face of God that old man, and turning to the earth from which I was taken. Earth therefore I shall eat all the days of my life, and earth I work, and this sending up thorns and thistles to me, my griefs and shameful cares, having let go the fine and good cares. And to what I had left, to these again turning: the land whence I came out, and my kindred below, and into the house of my father; having left the good land, where the good fatherland, being mine, was long unknown to me; and kinsmen whom having as intimates of my soul, later I began to know; and the house of the one truly our father, in which abiding, by the true sons who wish to remain in it, the father is reverently honored and revered. But I, unreverent and unworthy, go out from these, turned to the things behind, and running back. A certain son is said, receiving from a father the portion falling to him against his other brother, to have gone abroad from the father into a far country, having wished this; living prodigally, to have scattered the paternal substance and consumed it; at last in want, having hired himself to herd swine; compelled by famine to desire to share the food of the swine, but not to obtain even this. So he paid the penalty of his prodigal table, having exchanged for the paternal [table], being royal, [foods] which he did not foresee, the swinish and the hireling foods. Some such thing we seem about to suffer having departed, and not even with all the falling portion. For not even having received what was needed; yet we depart. Having left the fine and dear things with you and beside you, having exchanged for the worse. For all gloomy things will succeed us: noise and confusion out of peace, and out of quiet and orderly, a disordered life. Out of this freedom, harsh slavery: markets and lawsuits, crowds and luxury, and leisure for us no longer for the better things, not any at all. Nor shall we speak the divine oracles; we shall speak the works of men. (This indeed simply a curse was held to be for a prophet man.) But we, also of wicked men. Night truly from day, from bright light darkness, from festival mourning, from fatherland a hostile country will succeed us, in which a sacred song it is not permitted me to sing. For how in a land foreign of my soul? Where, remaining, it is not possible to sing to God; only to weep and groan, being reminded of the things here, if anyone will concede even this to me. Enemies once are said, having come upon a great and holy city, in which the divine was served, to have dragged down as captives the inhabitants, both hymn-singers and God-speakers, into their country; it was Babylonia; those carried into it, not even being asked by the rulers, [were not] willing to hymn the divine nor to sing psalms in the profane [land]; but to have hung the musical instruments on the willows, being idle, and themselves to weep by the rivers of Babylon. One of those I seem to be, being driven from a city, and this my fatherland, and holy, where by day and night the sacred laws are proclaimed, hymns and songs and mystic words; and the sunlight and the continuous waking-vision of day, while we commune with the divine mysteries, and by night, of what the soul saw and did in the day, held by the images. And wholly, to sum up, where the God-filled possession is constant, from this I am driven out, carried captive into the foreign land. Where neither to play the flute will be permitted me, having hung my instrument, as also they, from the willows. But by the rivers I shall be, and clay I shall work, and to say hymns I shall not wish, remembering; but perhaps from the long labor at other things I shall even forget, robbed as to memories. And if even, departing, unwilling only like a captive, yet also willing I depart, not by any other but by myself warred out, it being possible perhaps to remain. And departing from here, I shall not travel safely, as having gone out from a safe and peaceful city. Likely that, journeying, I shall meet with robbers and be seized, and stripped I shall be wounded with many wounds, and shall lie somewhere thrown down half dead.

pass_b_english: This is truly a paradise of delight; this is true gladness and delight, the delight we have enjoyed in this time now completed. It has been no short time already, and yet it is short altogether, if it is to stop here, now that we are leaving and withdrawing from this place. For I do not know what has happened to me, or what sin I have committed again, that I am going out, that I am being driven out. What I ought to say I do not know, except that I am a second Adam out of paradise (Genesis 3:23–24), and I have begun to talk. How well off I was while I listened to my teacher speaking and kept silent! Would that I were keeping quiet even now! I was learning while I kept silent. If only I had not put on this novel spectacle, making my teacher the listener! What need did I have of these words? Why should I address such things to you at all? What was needed was not to go away, but to stay on. But these faults seem to belong to the ancient deception, and these penalties for the ancient wrongs still await me. Or else I seem to myself to be disobeying once more, daring to go beyond the words of God, when I ought to remain in them and beside them.

And I am going away, fleeing from this blessed life no less than that man of old fled from the face of God (Genesis 3:8), and returning to the earth from which I was taken (Genesis 3:19). So I shall eat earth all the days of my life (Genesis 3:17), and I work the earth (Genesis 3:23), an earth that brings forth thorns and thistles for me (Genesis 3:18): my own griefs and shameful cares, now that I have let go of noble and good cares. And I am turning back again to the things I had left behind: to the land from which I came out, to my kindred here below, and to the house of my father (Genesis 12:1). I am leaving the good land, where my good homeland lay, though for a long time I did not know it; and the kinsmen whom I had as kindred of my soul, though only later did I begin to know them; and the house of him who is truly our father, where he abides and where the father is reverently honored and revered by the true sons who wish to remain in it. But I, without reverence and unworthy, go out from these things, turning back toward what lies behind and running back the way I came.

There is a story of a son who received from his father the share of the inheritance that fell to him, as against his other brother, and went abroad from his father into a far country, by his own choice. Living wastefully, he scattered his father's property and used it up. At last, in his want, he hired himself out to feed swine. Driven by hunger, he longed even to share the swine's food, yet he could not get even this (Luke 15:12–16). So he paid the penalty for his wasteful table: in exchange for his father's table, which was a royal one, he received what he had not foreseen, the food of swine and the food of a hired laborer. Something like this, it seems, we too shall suffer in going away, and not even with the whole share that falls to us. For we have not even received what we ought, and yet we are going all the same. We leave the good and dear things with you and beside you, and take the worse in exchange.

For in their place everything gloomy will come upon us: uproar and confusion after peace, and after a quiet and orderly life, a disordered one; after this freedom, a harsh slavery: market-places and lawsuits, crowds and luxury. We shall no longer have the least leisure for better things. We shall not speak the divine oracles; we shall speak the works of men (Psalm 17:4). (A prophet held this to be nothing less than a curse.) And in our case it will be the works of wicked men. Truly, for us night will follow day, darkness will follow shining light, mourning will follow festival, and a hostile country will follow our homeland, where I may not sing a sacred song. For how could I sing in a land foreign to my soul (Psalm 137:4)? There, while we stay, we cannot sing to God; we can only weep and groan as we remember what is here (Psalm 137:1), if anyone will grant me even this.

Enemies, we are told, once came against a great and holy city in which God was worshipped, and dragged off its inhabitants as captives, singers of hymns and those who spoke of God, to their own country, which was Babylon. And those who were carried there were not willing to hymn God, even when their masters asked them (Psalm 137:3), or to sing psalms in a profane land. Instead, now idle, they hung their musical instruments on the willows, and they themselves wept by the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137:1–2). I seem to be one of them, driven out of a city, out of this sacred homeland of mine. Here by day and night the sacred laws are declared, and hymns and songs and mystical words. Here there is the light of the sun and an unbroken waking vision by day, as we converse with the divine mysteries, and by night we are held by the images of what the soul saw and did by day. In short, this is where the inspiration of God holds us at every moment; from this I am driven out, carried off a captive into a foreign land. There I shall not even be allowed to play the flute, for I shall have hung my instrument on the willows as they did (Psalm 137:2). I shall be by the rivers and shall work in clay, and I shall not wish to recite hymns, though I remember them; and perhaps, through long labor at other things, I shall even forget, robbed of my memories.

And if only, in going, I went merely against my will, like a captive! But I go willingly too, driven out not by anyone else but by my own warfare against myself, when perhaps I could stay. And once I leave here, I shall not travel in safety, as one who has gone out from a city that is safe and at peace. It is likely that on the road I shall fall in with robbers and be seized, and be stripped and wounded with many wounds, and lie somewhere, thrown down half dead (Luke 10:30).
notes: Psalm numbering: 'speak the works of men' answers Psalm 16:4 in the LXX ('that my mouth may not speak the works of men'), Psalm 17:4 in English Bibles; the Babylon passage follows LXX Psalm 136:1-4, English Psalm 137:1-4 (captors asking for songs is 137:3). 'Paradise of delight' (παράδεισος τρυφῆς) is the LXX name for Eden (Genesis 3:23-24); the expulsion is cited once at 'a second Adam out of paradise'. 'Eat earth all the days of my life' uses the wording God speaks to the serpent in LXX Genesis 3:14 (γῆν φάγῃ πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς σου) but is applied to Adam's sentence, where 3:17 has 'in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life' (Gregory's next word is λύπας, griefs); cited as Genesis 3:17, with 3:14 noted here. 'Work the earth' (3:23) is present tense in the Greek (ἐργάζομαι) beside the future ἔδομαι; the English keeps the present. The reversal of Abraham's call (land, kindred, father's house) is cited as Genesis 12:1. Left uncited as uncertain: 'the ancient deception' (the serpent's deceit, Genesis 3:13, no shared wording beyond ἀπάτη); 'turning back toward what lies behind' (τὰ ὀπίσω; Luke 9:62 or Philippians 3:13 possible); 'by day and night' (Psalm 1:2 possible); 'work in clay' (Israel's bondage, Exodus 1:14, possible); forgetting (Psalm 137:5 possible). Ambiguities: 'the house of him who is truly our father' most naturally means Origen as spiritual father, whose house is the school Gregory is leaving (the prodigal comparison then says 'we leave the good things with you'); it could be read of God, so 'father' is kept lower case and not capitalized. 'The penalties of the ancient wrongs' renders τῶν ἀρχαίων δίκαι, where τῶν ἀρχαίων may be neuter (ancient deeds) or masculine (the first parents). 'τῶν δὴ' after ἐξέρχομαι is read as 'from these things' (the print's τ-compendium; τὸ δὴ possible). 'μηδ᾽ ἀξιουμένους ὑπὸ τῶν κρατούντων' is taken as 'even when their masters asked them', matching Psalm 137:3. 'κατακωχή' (print; marginal ἴσ. κατοχή not adopted) is rendered 'inspiration of God holds us', the Platonic sense of being possessed by a god. The last paragraph's opening 'Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀπιών, ἄκων μόνον ὥσπερ αἰχμάλωτος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑκὼν ἄπειμι' is elliptical; it is read as an unfinished wish ('if only I went merely unwillingly ... but I go willingly too'), as the facing Latin of the Paris 1622 print takes it ('Quod si abiens, inuitus abirem, ut captiui solent: at volens abeo'). ἐκπεπολεμημένος ('warred out') is rendered 'driven out ... by my own warfare against myself'. χλιδή is rendered 'luxury' (Latin 'deliciae'). The nominative ὑπομιμνησκόμενοι after the generic accusative μένοντας is taken as first person ('we can only weep ... as we remember'). 'ἐμάνθανον σιωπῶν, ἀλλὰ μὴ ... ποιήσασθαι': the negative infinitive is taken under the preceding ὄφελον ('If only I had not put on this novel spectacle'). 'Eat earth all the days of my life' is cited as Genesis 3:17 with the Genesis 3:14 wording noted above.
